name: Society, Population & Social Change
description: Iranian society is shaped by changing population patterns, urban settlement, family relationships, migration, and unequal access to work and services. Understanding these changes requires attention to differences between generations, places, and residents with different legal and economic circumstances.

seo.title: Iranian Society, Population and Social Change | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore how demography, cities, migration, family life, employment and unequal access to services shape social change in Iran.

content.heading: Reading society through connected changes
content.content:
Iran's social transformation cannot be reduced to a single national average. Population ageing, changing households, urban settlement, and access to employment operate together, but their consequences vary between communities. The World Bank's historical poverty diagnostic connects these developments while documenting differences in welfare between households and regions. Its findings describe the period studied rather than a timeless portrait of Iranian life. [s1]

This directory approaches society through seven connected subjects: demography, migration, urbanization, family relationships, employment and welfare, social challenges, and regional communities. These branches answer different questions. Demography examines population composition; migration examines movement; welfare research asks how people obtain resources and protection. A change in one does not establish an equivalent improvement in another.

content.heading: An urban majority with substantial regional differences
content.content:
The selected results of Iran's 2016 Population and Housing Census show why place matters. Table 5 reports a national urbanization rate of 74%, compared with 94% in Tehran province and 48% in Sistan and Baluchestan. These are provincial shares of residents classified as urban, not the populations of the cities of Tehran or Zahedan. Nor does urban classification measure the quality of housing, public transport, or employment. [s2]

A national urban majority therefore leaves considerable variation to explain. Regional and community studies help connect settlement patterns to local circumstances. Readers should distinguish a province, a city within it, and the surrounding metropolitan area: their boundaries and populations answer different questions. The census publication itself separates urban, rural, and unsettled populations, preserving distinctions that disappear when all residents are described simply as city dwellers. [s2]

content.heading: Families and the movement of generations
content.content:
Households connect population change with everyday responsibilities. The World Bank's diagnostic describes smaller households alongside urbanization and an older population. A household, however, is a statistical unit rather than a complete map of kinship. Its size alone cannot tell us who provides care, how relatives share money, or whether family members live nearby. Those questions require evidence about relationships and arrangements, not just a headcount. [s1]

Ageing also concerns people well before old age. UNFPA, the United Nations Population Fund, advocates a life-course approach in Iran: health, participation, accessibility, and support should be considered across successive stages of life. Its ageing programme identifies gaps in welfare and social systems as research priorities. This approach treats older people as members of communities with different capabilities and circumstances, rather than assuming that everyone beyond an age threshold has identical needs. [s3]

content.heading: Migration, documentation and access
content.content:
Migration includes moves within Iran as well as movement across its borders. International displacement adds a distinct legal dimension. UNHCR's 2025 annual results report distinguishes recognized refugees from other forcibly displaced residents with different documentation. It describes both access to public services and continuing protection concerns, including the consequences of documentation changes and return procedures. Its account supports neither an assumption of universal exclusion nor an assumption that formal inclusion removes practical barriers. [s4]

Education illustrates the difference between eligibility and effective access. UNICEF identifies overcrowding, limited school space, economic and geographical obstacles, transport difficulties, and gender disparities among the barriers affecting children in Iran. Its programme describes intended responses; those objectives should not be mistaken for independently demonstrated nationwide results. The useful question is whether a child can attend and learn consistently, alongside the formal question of admission. [s5]

content.heading: Employment is one part of social security
content.content:
Employment research must distinguish unemployment from participation. Someone outside the labour force is not counted as unemployed merely because they have no job. The World Bank's historical diagnostic describes how withdrawal from job-seeking complicated interpretation of labour-market conditions during the COVID-19 crisis. A falling unemployment rate, considered alone, consequently cannot establish that more people obtained paid work. [s1]

Welfare analysis also needs to distinguish a statistical poverty threshold from wider experiences of insecurity. The World Bank's Poverty and Inequality Platform labels its international thresholds, purchasing-power basis, and reference years explicitly. These are essential qualifications: a poverty estimate for an earlier survey year does not measure conditions on the day a webpage is accessed, and an international threshold is not automatically Iran's national poverty line. [s6]

content.heading: Following the evidence
content.content:
A useful reading of social change moves between national patterns and local experience. The demography branch explains population measures; migration and urbanization examine movement and settlement; family and community studies investigate relationships that aggregate statistics cannot fully describe. Employment, welfare, and social-challenge pages then examine how resources and opportunities are distributed.

Evidence quality remains part of the subject. UNFPA identifies opportunities to improve integration of Iranian statistical sources and harmonization of civil registration with other data. Readers should therefore check the reference period, population covered, and method before treating apparently conflicting figures as contradictory. A census count, a household survey result, and a modelled population estimate can all be useful while measuring different things. [s7]

name: Demography
description: Demography examines the size, composition and distribution of Iran's population through births, deaths, migration and the passage of generations. Census results, registration records and population estimates provide complementary evidence, but their definitions and reference periods must remain distinct.

seo.title: Demography of Iran: Population, Fertility and Ageing | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Understand Iran's demographic transition and learn how census counts, fertility, life expectancy, age structure and migration fit together.

content.heading: Population is a stock; demographic events are flows
content.content:
Demography studies how populations change and how their members are distributed by characteristics such as age and place of residence. Births add people, deaths remove them, and migration changes where people live. Age structure records the cumulative consequences of these processes as successive generations grow older. Research on Iran's demographic transition therefore examines fertility, mortality, and migration together. [s1]

A population total is not an annual number of births, and a movement across a provincial boundary is not necessarily international migration. These distinctions matter when reading Iranian statistics: a national population can change while particular provinces follow different trajectories. The relevant denominator and geographical boundary belong beside the result, rather than being left for readers to infer. [s1]

content.heading: What fertility measures
content.content:
Total fertility rate summarizes a year's age-specific childbearing rates as births per woman. It describes a hypothetical lifetime under those rates, rather than counting the children already born to the average woman. It must also be distinguished from the number of births registered during the year. The latter depends on how many women are at childbearing ages as well as their childbearing rates. [s2]

This helps explain population momentum: earlier growth can leave numerous people entering childbearing ages, sustaining births even after fertility declines. The United Nations identifies momentum from past growth as a major demographic mechanism internationally. Applying that principle does not establish an exact date when Iran's population will peak; such a date requires a specified projection and its assumptions. [s3]

content.heading: Life expectancy is a period measure
content.content:
Life expectancy at birth summarizes the mortality conditions prevailing across age groups in a particular period. It asks how long a newborn would live if those death rates continued. It is neither a prediction of an individual child's lifespan nor the average age of people who died that year. [s4]

The distinction is especially useful when examining sudden mortality changes. A period indicator can worsen during a crisis without implying that everyone permanently loses the same number of years of life. Conversely, an improvement in the national measure does not demonstrate that all places or social groups experience identical survival conditions. The underlying age-specific rates and population coverage remain essential to interpretation. [s4]

content.heading: From demographic transition to an older population
content.content:
UNFPA describes Iran as having reached low fertility and mortality and identifies population ageing as a major planning issue. Ageing concerns the changing balance of age groups, rather than a claim that children or young adults have disappeared. Its implications include the accessibility of services and the ability of welfare systems to respond to different needs across life. [s5]

A large population at conventional working ages can create an economic opportunity, but it does not itself produce employment. Stanford's Iran 2040 research stresses the importance of jobs, skills, and economic conditions in converting demographic circumstances into benefits. Its projections belong to their publication vintage; they should not be presented as newly verified forecasts for October 2026. [s1]

content.title: How demographic change fits together
content.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["Population at the beginning of a period"] -->|"Starting stock"| E["Population at the end of the period"]
  B["Births during the period"] -->|"Add residents"| E
  C["Deaths during the period"] -->|"Subtract residents"| E
  D["Immigration minus emigration"] -->|"Add net migration"| E
  E -->|"Classify residents by age"| F["Population age structure"]
```
content.summary: This is a conceptual population-accounting diagram. It distinguishes the population stock from demographic flows; it does not estimate their size or imply that statistical revisions never occur.

content.heading: Counts, estimates and the limits of comparison
content.content:
Iran's census summaries provide dated snapshots, including age and settlement information. International annual estimates answer a different need: they provide population series between enumerations using demographic evidence and methods. UNFPA identifies harmonization of civil registration and other statistical sources as an area for improvement. A difference between published totals therefore needs investigation before being interpreted as an error. [s6]

The pages below separate age structure, fertility, life expectancy, ageing, provincial distribution, and household change. Together they provide a framework for reading demographic claims without confusing a modelled estimate with a census count or a future scenario with an observed outcome.

name: Population Age Structure
description: Iran's population age structure describes how residents are distributed across age groups. Annual estimates show that the share aged under fifteen rose slightly during the mid-2010s before declining, while broader age categories require careful interpretation when discussing employment and dependency.

seo.title: Iran's Population Age Structure and Child Population Share | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Examine Iran's annual child-population share, understand age groups and distinguish demographic dependency from economic participation.

content.heading: What an age structure describes
content.content:
Population age structure shows the distribution of residents across ages, rather than simply how many people live in a country. Common broad categories distinguish children, conventional working ages, and older residents. These boundaries make comparisons possible, but they are analytical conventions: they do not establish whether a particular person attends school, works, receives a pension, or provides care. [s1]

The World Bank's age-dependency definition is particularly explicit about this limitation. It compares residents below fifteen and above sixty-four with those aged fifteen to sixty-four. The resulting ratio describes age composition, not actual economic dependency. Some people outside the conventional working-age band work, while some inside it do not. [s1]

content.heading: A recent pattern with a modest reversal
content.content:
The annual series below measures the percentage of Iran's population aged zero through fourteen. It is not a birth rate or an absolute count of children. The observations show a small increase during the middle of the displayed period followed by a decline. Thus, describing every recent year as a continuous fall would obscure the actual pattern. [s2]

A falling share does not, by itself, establish that the number of children fell: the total population is the denominator. It also cannot isolate the contribution of births, survival, or migration. The indicator is useful for describing composition, while explaining its causes requires additional demographic evidence. [s2, s3]

content.title: Iran: population aged 0–14 as a share of total population, 2012–2026
content.interpretation: The displayed share rises modestly into 2018 and then declines through 2025. The final year has no inspected observation and remains a gap; the published values are demographic estimates rather than annual census counts. [s2]

content.title: Published annual child-population shares and the unfilled 2026 observation

content.heading: Keeping age thresholds and sources consistent
content.content:
A discussion of older residents must retain its age threshold. A measure beginning at sixty includes people excluded from a measure beginning at sixty-five; the two cannot be exchanged without changing the population being described. Similarly, a share of the national population cannot be compared directly with a dependency ratio whose denominator is only the conventional working-age population. [s1]

The World Bank identifies the United Nations Population Division's World Population Prospects as the source for its child-share indicator. The annual values inspected here were distributed through FRED, the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis's economic database. Their many decimal places should not be read as evidence of equally precise enumeration: these are published demographic series, subject to their source methods and later revisions. [s2, s3]

content.heading: What this measure can support
content.content:
Age composition helps frame questions about infrastructure and service needs. It does not determine the answer: the same population share can correspond to different absolute populations, settlement patterns, and participation rates. The World Bank's metadata specifically distinguishes demographic dependency from economic dependency and notes the planning relevance of age structure. [s1]

The child-share series is therefore a starting point. A fuller assessment should add compatible counts and other age groups from the same statistical vintage, then examine regional differences. This page does not infer the older-population share by subtracting the child share alone, or turn an age category into an employment estimate.

datasets.methodology: World Development Indicators indicator SP.POP.0014.TO.ZS, distributed by FRED as SPPOP0014TOZSIRN. The share is the population aged 0–14 divided by total population, expressed on a 0–100 percentage scale. World Bank identifies United Nations World Population Prospects as the underlying source. Values are transcribed at published precision without author interpolation or rounding. FRED's January 1 dates identify annual observations and are not treated here as evidence of an enumeration on that date; exact reference boundaries remain null. All numeric observations are classified as source estimates. The inspected distribution does not identify the estimate-versus-projection boundary or scenario for its latest observation; 2025 must not be described as an observed census result. The requested default window is 2012–2026, with 2026 explicitly missing.
